sources.title: THE EVIDENCE OF THE PERSEPOLIS TABLETS
sources.locator: R. T. Hallock, chapter 11 in The Cambridge History of Iran (1985), pp. 588–609. Public Summary, third paragraph, web lines 480–481; metadata lines 499–505. Only the public summary was read, not the access-controlled chapter.
sources.asWorded: thirtieth year of Darius I to the seventh year of Artaxerxes I (492–45 8 B.C.)
sources.originalChronology: The publisher summary gives 492–458 BCE, with an extraction space in 458. The original regnal endpoints are retained without a new conversion.
sources.scopedClaim: Treasury documents record silver disbursements replacing part, and rarely all, of rations. This describes attested payments, not the origin of wages or a universal monetary reform.
sources.reuseTerms: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

sources.title: The Ritual Landscape at Persepolis: Glyptic Imagery from the Persepolis Fortification and Treasury Archives
sources.institution: Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, University of Chicago
sources.locator: Public publisher description of Mark B. Garrison's 2017 book, Studies in Ancient Oriental Civilization 72; second descriptive paragraph, web line 380. Author and publication metadata at lines 368 and 402–405. The book itself was not read.
sources.originalChronology: The description gives 492–457 BCE for the Treasury archive and 509–493 BCE for the separate Fortification archive. No explanation for the difference from Hallock's 458 endpoint is supplied here.
sources.scopedClaim: The Treasury archive is an administrative tablet corpus with a published date span of 492–457 BCE. This source supports chronology, not an independently inspected payment text or workers' legal status.
sources.reuseTerms: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

date.noteEn: These are published spans of the Treasury records, not a reform's start and end. Hallock gives Darius I's year 30 through Artaxerxes I's year 7 as 492–458 BCE; Garrison's publisher gives 492–457. The full envelope preserves both endpoints without assuming uninterrupted payments.

events.titleEn: Persepolis records silver payments against rations
events.summaryEn: Treasury records document silver disbursements in place of part, and occasionally all, of ration payments. They provide evidence of royal payment administration at Persepolis.
events.selectionNote: A notable administrative practice documented over a dated interval, distinct from the city's later burning. The record does not announce an invented reform, the first wages, universal coin payment or a conclusion about workers' freedom. Both accounts concern the same archive, and their endpoints differ by one year.
